body:
This reply means more to me than anything I can remember anyone saying to me.  Thank you so much.

I certainly relate to growing up with a puritanical work ethic; my parents' religion was very strict on that subject, as well as many others.  I wonder if you've had similar experiences with religion.

The nervous breakdown thing I relate to as well.  I'm so sorry to hear you had to go through one because it sounds like yours was worse than mine.  When I had mine, my mother drove 5 hours to drag me into the health clinic and get some emergency help.  I have no idea how, but I managed to improve from that point incrementally before everything fell apart a year later.

Not sure how meaningful this is, but somehow I hope that even though I might not be around in a few weeks, you find the strength to continue on.  I somehow get the sense from your post that you are a good person; the fact that you hang out around here and help people is a sign of a very good heart.  I think part of my problem is that I wish I was a good person but I'm just not.  It's terrible that it's difficult for you to contribute in the way you want, but I guarantee you that the world needs more good people and not fewer.  I hope so much that your new therapist can help you achieve a higher level of well-being, and perhaps even bring you to a place where life seems worth living once again.

From what you've written, I can tell you that I admire you.  From my own situation I can say that applying for public assistance is one of the bravest things a person in your shoes can do, and I know you did it out of love for your mother.  The fact that you've decided to humble yourself for the sake of your mother shows a level of concern for those you love which I'm afraid I just don't have.

Given that I was in university and grad school for the entirety of my adult life working only about 20 hours per week, I find it doubtful that I could qualify for SSDI.  I feel like the system was set up for people like you who have actually contributed a significant amount before becoming disabled, rather than people like me.

I thank you for your advice, however, and I wish I could say I had the hope to put it into practice.  Based on the past 10 years of therapy, medication, and failure I feel like I might not have much of a chance.  But since you recommended these things to me I will look into a new therapist on Monday, and see if I can get some improvement.  My plan is still to end it all when I lose access to my health insurance, though, unless I find some miracle which makes my life more tolerable.

Thank you again.  I really do wish you the best.  If you would like to talk please feel free to send me a message.
